units.title: Unit 8: Electric Charges, Fields, and Gauss's Law

subtopics.title: Electric Charge and Electric Force, part 1

outcomes.text: Describe the electric force that results from interactions between charged objects or systems.
Treat charge as a fundamental scalar property that is positive or negative, with elementary charge e and the point-charge model.
Apply Coulomb's law: force grows with each charge and falls with the square of distance.
Give the direction of electrostatic force along the line between objects: like repel, unlike attract.
Explain that everyday contact forces come from many electric interactions.

subtopics.title: Electric Charge and Electric Force, part 2

outcomes.text: Compare electric and gravitational forces on charged objects with mass.
Contrast electric forces that attract or repel with gravity that only attracts.
Recognize that gravity is usually far weaker than electric force between charged masses.
Explain why gravity dominates at large scales: large systems are nearly neutral.

subtopics.title: Electric Charge and Electric Force, part 3

outcomes.text: Describe the electric permittivity of a material or medium.
Define permittivity as how strongly a medium polarizes in a field.
Model polarization as induced rearrangement of electrons separating charge.
Use the constant permittivity of free space in physical relationships.
Explain how matter's permittivity differs from free space and how conductors and insulators differ.

topics.title: 8.2 Conservation of Electric Charge and the Process of Charging

subtopics.title: Conservation of Electric Charge and the Process of Charging

outcomes.text: Describe system behavior using conservation of charge.
Explain how friction, contact and induced charge separation change a system's charge or distribution.
Attribute any net charge change to charge transfer, typically electrons, with net charge otherwise constant.
Define grounding as connecting a charged object to a huge, nearly neutral system such as Earth.
Describe the electric field produced by a charged object or configuration of point charges.
State that electric fields originate from charged objects.
Define the field as force per unit test charge and give its direction relative to positive and negative charges.
Treat the field as a vector: add fields from several charges and read field maps and field-line diagrams.
Describe the electric field generated by charged conductors or insulators.
Explain that in equilibrium a conductor's excess charge sits on its surface with zero interior field, perpendicular at the surface, and a sphere acts like a point charge outside.
Explain that an insulator's excess charge can be throughout its interior with a nonzero interior field.
Describe the electric field resulting from a given charge distribution.
Find fields of charge distributions by integration and superposition.
Use symmetry to simplify field calculations.
Describe the electric flux through an arbitrary area or shape.
Describe flux as the amount of a quantity passing through an area.
Compute flux for a constant field using the area vector and dot product, with sign from orientation.
Define total flux as the surface integral of the field.
Describe properties of a charge distribution by applying Gauss's law.
State Gauss's law: flux through a Gaussian surface relates to enclosed charge.
Define a Gaussian surface as a closed three-dimensional surface.
Note that total flux depends only on enclosed charge, not surface size.
Choose Gaussian surfaces where the field is perpendicular or parallel to simplify the integral.
Integrate a charge density over length, area or volume to get total charge.
Identify Gauss's law as the first of Maxwell's equations.
Describe the electric potential energy of a system.
Define potential energy of two point charges as the work to bring them from infinity to their positions.
Use the general equation for electric potential energy between two charged objects.
Sum the pair-by-pair energies to get a system's total electric potential energy.
Describe the electric potential due to a configuration of charged objects.
Define electric potential as potential energy per unit charge at a point.
Find potential of charge distributions by integration and scalar superposition, including point charges.
Define potential difference as the change in potential energy per unit test charge.
Note that chemical processes, as in a battery, can also separate charge to create potential difference.
Describe the relationship between electric potential and electric field.
Relate a field component to the negative spatial rate of change of potential.
Find potential difference by integrating the field along a path.
Use field maps and equipotential lines, perpendicular to the field, to predict motion; fields point toward decreasing potential.
Describe changes in a system due to a potential difference between two locations.
Compute the potential energy change of a charge moving between points of different potential.
Link that change to the charge's kinetic energy change by energy conservation.
Describe the charge distribution within a conductor.
Define an ideal conductor as a material whose electrons move freely.
Explain that excess charge of a conductor in equilibrium resides entirely on its surface.
Explain equilibrium: it forms almost instantly, the surface is equipotential, and charge density is higher at points and edges.
State that the interior has no net charge and zero electric field.
State that the field is perpendicular to the conductor's outer surface.
Explain that an external field polarizes a conductor while it stays equipotential.
Describe electrostatic shielding by a closed conducting shell.
Describe charge movement and interactions when conductors touch.
Explain that touching conductors share charge until their surfaces reach the same potential.
Define ground as an ideal zero-potential reference that can take or supply unlimited charge.
Explain inducing charge on a conductor by grounding it in an external field.
Describe the physical properties of a parallel-plate capacitor.
Describe a capacitor as two separated conducting surfaces holding equal and opposite charge.
Define capacitance as charge per potential difference, depending on geometry and material, and find it for parallel plates.
Describe the nearly uniform field between charged plates, found with Gauss's law, and a charge's constant acceleration in it.
Equate stored energy with the work to separate the charge.
Compute the energy stored in a capacitor.
Describe how a dielectric between capacitor plates changes the capacitor.
Explain that a dielectric polarizes in an external field because charges are less free than in a conductor.
Define the dielectric constant as relating a material's permittivity to free space.
Explain that a polarized dielectric's field opposes the external field.
Show that the field in an isolated capacitor decreases when a dielectric is inserted.
Show that inserting a dielectric can change the capacitance.
Describe the movement of electric charges through a medium.
Define current as charge passing a wire cross-section per time, via drift velocity, driven by emf.
Define current density as current per unit area, linked to carrier motion and to field via resistivity.
Integrate current density over area to get total current.
Explain current's direction as conventional (positive charge) and that it is a scalar without vector addition.
Describe the behavior of a circuit.
List the elements that make up circuits.
Distinguish closed, open and short circuits in closed loops.
Recognize that one element can belong to several loops.
Use circuit schematics and standard symbols, with conventional current.
Describe the resistance of an object using its physical properties.
Define resistance as opposition to charge movement.
Relate resistance to resistivity, length and cross-sectional area, including varying resistivity and temperature effects.
Describe the electrical characteristics of circuit elements.
Apply Ohm's law to ohmic elements, their constant resistance, heating, and slope of current versus voltage.
Describe energy transfer in a circuit in terms of power.
Compute power from current and potential difference.
Predict lightbulb brightness from power.
Describe the equivalent resistance of multiple resistors.
Distinguish series connections (same current) from parallel (same potential difference).
Find equivalent resistance: sum for series, reciprocal sum for parallel, which lowers with more paths.
Describe a circuit with resistive wires and a battery with internal resistance.
Treat ideal batteries and wires as resistance-free and know when wire resistance can be ignored, and the meaning of emf.
Model internal resistance as a series resistor with an ideal battery.
Explain that terminal voltage drops below emf when current flows through internal resistance.
Describe the measurement of current and potential difference in a circuit.
Connect ammeters in series; ideal ones have zero resistance.
Connect voltmeters in parallel; ideal ones have infinite resistance.
Recognize that nonideal meters alter the circuit measured.
Describe a circuit by applying Kirchhoff's loop rule.
Represent circuit energy changes as charges moving through potential differences.
Apply the loop rule, a consequence of energy conservation: potential differences around a loop sum to zero, and graph potential around a loop.
Describe a circuit by applying Kirchhoff's junction rule.
Explain the junction rule as a consequence of charge conservation.
Apply the rule: current entering a junction equals current leaving.
Describe the equivalent capacitance of multiple capacitors.
Find equivalent capacitance: reciprocal sum for series (below the smallest) and plain sum for parallel.
Explain that series capacitors hold the same charge by charge conservation.
Describe the behavior of circuits with resistors and capacitors.
Describe RC charge or current by a differential equation from the loop rule.
Define the time constant and its 63 and 37 percent meanings for charging and discharging.
Describe how capacitor voltage, current and energy change over time toward steady state, including early and late behavior.
Describe the properties of a magnetic field.
Describe the magnetic field as a vector field acting on moving charges, currents and magnetic materials, produced by dipoles never monopoles.
Represent the field as a vector quantity with field maps.
State that field lines form closed loops (Gauss's law for magnetism, Maxwell's second equation).
Describe a material's magnetic behavior from its dipole configuration.
Explain dipoles from circular charge motion, permanent versus induced magnetism, no isolated poles, and pole attraction and repulsion.
Explain that a compass dipole aligns with a magnetic field.
Distinguish ferromagnetic, paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials.
Approximate Earth's field as a magnetic dipole.
Describe the magnetic permeability of a material.
Define permeability as magnetization in response to an external field.
Use the constant vacuum permeability.
Explain that matter's permeability differs from free space and varies with conditions.
Describe the magnetic field produced by moving charged objects.
Explain that a moving charge makes a field depending on velocity and distance, perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule, strongest when they are perpendicular.
Describe the force a magnetic field exerts on moving charged objects.
Compute magnetic force from the cross product of velocity and field.
Treat electric and magnetic forces on a moving charge as independent.
Describe the Hall effect as a potential difference across a conductor in a perpendicular field.

topics.title: 12.3 Magnetic Fields of Current-Carrying Wires and the Biot-Savart Law

subtopics.title: Magnetic Fields of Current-Carrying Wires and the Biot-Savart Law

outcomes.text: Describe the magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire.
Use the Biot-Savart law for field magnitude and direction from current.
Describe field vectors around a wire segment as tangent to concentric circles.
Derive fields of wire segments, such as at the center of a circular loop.
Describe the force a magnetic field exerts on current-carrying wires.
State that a magnetic field exerts force on a current-carrying wire.
Use Ampere's law to describe the magnetic field created by a moving charge carrier.
Relate field to enclosed current around an Amperian loop, for long wires and long solenoids.
Define an Amperian loop as a closed path around a current-carrying conductor.
Use superposition to combine fields of several conductors, loops, segments or cylinders.
Identify Ampere's law with Maxwell's addition as Maxwell's fourth equation: changing electric fields create magnetic fields.
Describe the magnetic flux through an arbitrary area or shape.
Compute flux for a constant field using the area vector and dot product, with sign from orientation.
Define total flux as the surface integral of the field.
Describe the induced potential difference from a change in magnetic flux.
Apply Faraday's law: induced emf from changing flux, whether field or area changes, times turns in a solenoid.
Use Lenz's law and the right-hand rule: induced current opposes the flux change.
Identify Faraday's law as Maxwell's third equation linking changing flux to induced electric field.
Recognize that Maxwell's equations imply electromagnetic waves at constant speed in free space.
Describe the force on a conductor from an external field acting on its induced current.
Explain that an external field exerts force on charge carriers in an induced-current loop.
Note forces act only on loop segments inside the field, causing translation or rotation.
Relate the force to induced current, flux change rate, loop resistance and velocity.
Apply Newton's second law to a loop moving in a field with induced emf.
Describe the physical and electrical properties of an inductor.
Define inductance as opposition to current change, and find a solenoid's inductance from its geometry and core.
Compute energy stored in an inductor's magnetic field and track where it goes.
Relate induced emf to inductance and the rate of change of current.

topics.title: 13.5 Circuits with Resistors and Inductors (LR Circuits)

subtopics.title: Circuits with Resistors and Inductors (LR Circuits)

outcomes.text: Describe a circuit with resistors and a single inductor.
Explain that resistors dissipate energy stored in an inductor as current changes.
Apply the loop rule to a series LR circuit to get the current's differential equation.
Define the LR time constant and its 63 and 37 percent meanings.
Describe inductor behavior over time: opposing initial change, exponential approach, then acting as a plain wire.

topics.title: 13.6 Circuits with Capacitors and Inductors (LC Circuits)

subtopics.title: Circuits with Capacitors and Inductors (LC Circuits)

outcomes.text: Describe a circuit with a single capacitor and inductor.
Find maximum inductor current in an LC circuit by energy conservation.
Model capacitor charge in an LC circuit as simple harmonic motion.
Derive the angular frequency of an LC circuit from its differential equation.
